rounds.question: What should the Logbook open on?
rounds.found: Every option opens on a front page: your top runs first, then cards for your best numbers, then THE FULL LOGBOOK for every entry (the contents). Move between the cards with the d-pad (up / down / left / right), A or a tap opens one and goes to its entry (the top runs open the top ten, your type opens your personality, best word opens best words with the breakdowns...), and B comes back to the front page where you were. The pictures and Play links use a made-up logbook so there's something to look at (it isn't saved). Also fixed in every version: you can always scroll back to the very top (the contents list's first line now scrolls all the way up).

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: the cover and the contents list.

options.title: Ledger
options.note: The title, then your top five runs as a bar chart (the high score's bar in red), then your numbers as boxed cards: your type, best word (spelled out in little keys), furthest night (with your recent runs charted), words sent (by length), most sent, longest word, favorite part, time on the air, every word. Each card opens its full entry; the last line opens the whole logbook.

options.title: Stamped
options.note: Your type stamped in red like a certificate next to your high score, a podium for your top three runs (4 and 5 under it), then the same numbers as index cards. The most 'look at me' of the three.

options.title: Chart
options.note: Your furthest night big, with a chart of your last 30 runs across the top, the top five as bars, then the numbers as one card per row: the name and a line on the left, a small picture in the middle, the number on the right. Most like a station's report sheet.

rounds.question: Stations: a retune tunes the radio to another song. Which stations should be in the rotation?
rounds.found: Each station has its own song, and the game's sounds (letter blips, the lock chime, the beacon, the tube, the count-up, lamps, night clear) move into that station's key and scale, so they stay in tune with whatever is playing. The beacon chime plays the chord the band is on right then. A retune fades the song out under the static and the next one starts on its first beat as the static clears, and the dial shows the station. The jazz ones are the four 'band in the next room' pieces from the music round, now with the sounds tuned to them; they also come through the wall a little clearer as the night's signal fills. Each clip is about 30 seconds: the station with three words played over it (letters, send, beacon, count-up) and a night clear at the end. 'Station tour' is all six in a row with real retunes between. Play: starts a run on that station; in these test copies you get 5 retunes a night and each one steps to the next station. Mark the ones to keep or cut in the notes, and say whether a retune should change the song, or each night, or both. The game itself doesn't change until you decide. Decided 2026-11-23: Last Call Trio is the second song (Chris liked its noir feel, and that it has hardly any tune, so your own sounds play the melody).

options.title: 540 kc: Night Pulse (now)
options.note: The game's own music, exactly as it is now: the slow A minor pulse, chord pads, soft beat. Everything else is tuned against this one.

options.title: 680 kc: Last Call Trio
options.note: Piano trio ballad at 70 BPM in D minor: brushes, upright bass, the piano taking the tune now and then. The game's sounds move up into D minor.

options.title: 880 kc: Blue Room Vibes
options.note: Very slow (62 BPM) and dreamy in E flat: vibraphone with its tremolo, soft bass, the lightest brushes. The sounds move into E flat.

options.title: 1010 kc: Muted Horn
options.note: A gentle swing at 92 BPM in C: walking bass, brushes and ride, piano chords, a cup-muted trumpet with short phrases. Same key as Night Pulse, so the sounds stay where they are.

options.title: 1240 kc: Old 78
options.note: 84 BPM, your tempo: the band with a clarinet as an old record from the next room, narrow, warm, crackling, wavering a little. In B flat; the sounds move down to match.

options.title: 1450 kc: Fog Pulse
options.note: Your idea of a second song with a new scale: the game's own band (same pads, bass and beat) with new chords in E dorian, minor with a raised sixth, a little lighter and mistier. The sounds move to E.

options.title: Station tour
options.note: All six in a row, about 14 seconds each, with a word played on each and a real retune into the next.

rounds.question: A third song: different from Night Pulse and Last Call Trio, still vibey. Which one?
rounds.found: Four new songs, each groove and chords with almost no tune, so your letters and chimes play the melody like they do over the trio. Your sounds move into each song's key and scale. New too: when a retune changes the station you hear the dial turning between stations (hiss sweeping up and back through a narrow band, whistles sliding past, crackle, a murmur from another station), then the new song comes in as it settles. 'Dial tour' starts on the trio and turns the dial through all four. Each clip is about 30 seconds with three words played over it. Play: starts on that song, with 5 retunes a night to go to the trio and Night Pulse and back. Decided 2026-11-23: none for now. The game keeps two stations, Night Pulse and Last Call Trio: each night starts on Night Pulse, a retune turns the dial to the other, and the next retune comes back.

options.title: 680 kc: Last Call Trio (your pick)
options.note: For comparison: the second song you picked.

options.title: 760 kc: Back Room Blues
options.note: A slow 12-bar blues in G after closing time: shuffled brushes, a walking bass, the piano answering on the off-beats. No tune at all. The game's sounds move to G, and its minor pentatonic is the blues scale's core, so the letters sound bluesy.

options.title: 1100 kc: Rain Bossa
options.note: A slow bossa nova in E minor at your 84 BPM: a nylon-string guitar picking the chords on the off-beats, a rim click playing the clave, a shaker, the bass rocking root and fifth. No tune. Lighter and warmer than the trio.

options.title: 920 kc: Palm Room
options.note: A 1950s hotel lounge in F minor: an organ holding the chords, hand drums and a shaker, a slow bolero bass, and the vibes ringing two chord notes now and then. Hazy and tropical, still at night.

options.title: 1350 kc: Midnight Serial
options.note: Between the scenes of an old radio mystery, in E phrygian (dark, with the half step above the root): an organ chord swelling on each change, a low drum under it, a clock ticking, and once in a while a far theremin sliding through two or three notes. The slowest and most suspenseful.

options.title: Dial tour
options.note: Last Call Trio, then the dial turning to each of the four new songs, about 14 seconds each.

rounds.question: Which lettering should the game use on its paper and brass (log, plates, sheets, menus)?
rounds.found: What the game uses now: our own 5x7 pixel 'ink' (log, labels, sheets), a bold doubled version 'key' (plates, titles: the 'big thick' one), lit dial dots (the dial, the night score, the run score drums), and two outside fonts only on the How to Play cards (Alfa Slab One titles, Special Elite text). Proposed rule: one lettering for everything printed on paper or brass, in two or three set sizes (small labels, figures, titles), and lit dots for anything that is a lit display. Each option shows the night report set in it (plates too). Pick one and it becomes the rule everywhere.

options.title: Small pixel ink (as now)
options.note: Our own 5x7 lettering, one small size for everything; values only stand out by color.

options.title: Our pixel ink, two sizes
options.note: The same thin lettering of ours, with figures half again as big. No new font, no thick type.

options.title: VT323
options.note: A thin, tall terminal font: reads like an old station readout. Free font, would be kept in the repo.

options.title: Pixelify Sans
options.note: A clean modern pixel font with a semibold for figures. Free font.

options.title: Silkscreen
options.note: Tiny square pixel capitals, very crisp, wide. Free font.

options.title: Special Elite
options.note: The typewriter face from the How to Play cards, for labels and figures alike (no slab).

rounds.question: Where should the run score show while you play, and how should it count up?
rounds.found: Four ways to keep the run score on screen while playing, in the part picker, the melter and the upgrade (it hides on the night report and DEAD AIR, which show it big). In all four, when a word's beam lands in the tube its points fly up as a '+N' into the counter, which counts up with a climbing tick and flares. Each counter grows a place when the score needs it (never fewer than 5) and shrinks to fit its corner if a score gets huge. Each clip sends RAT (+5), then shows a big +248 word's worth landing so you can see a long count. Play opens the game in that style with RAT traced.

options.title: Rolling drums
options.note: A brass-framed mechanical counter in the bottom-left corner of the room. Each drum turns up to the next figure as the score counts, the frame flares when it lands. Unused places show dim zeros.

options.title: Glow tubes
options.note: A small wooden case of glass tubes, each figure burning orange. Any figure that changes flares white-hot, then settles. A new tube lights up when the score needs another place.

options.title: Big lit dot display
options.note: The night report's lit dot-matrix figures, smaller, in a dark brass-rimmed panel in the corner. Counts in white-hot, settles to amber, with commas.

options.title: On the bar's brass plate
options.note: No new box: the lower brass plate in the bar shows the run score instead of the night number (the night is still announced at the start of each night and on the report). The plate glows and the figures pop while it counts.

rounds.question: How should the label on each part case look (NEW, STACKS X2, SWAP A PART, RARE: ONCE ONLY)?
rounds.found: The label used to sit over the case's bottom border and long ones ran off. Four ways to fix it. Each picture shows an overdrive picker with all four kinds of label: a part you already have (stacks), the rare Gold Key, and parts that need a swap (phone and Retroid) or are new (computer).

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: a dark chip low in the case that sits over its bottom border, and long labels run off it.

options.title: Brass tab
options.note: A small brass plate stamped with the label, sitting inside the case above its bottom border, like the name plate above it. Rare parts get a gold-tinted tab.

options.title: Dial window
options.note: A little dark lit window with the label in the radio's amber dot lights; rare parts get a gold rim and gold dots.

options.title: Lit line
options.note: No box at all: a thin brass rule near the foot of the case with the label lit underneath. The cleanest; rare parts get a gold rule.

options.title: Top badge
options.note: A rounded badge riding the top edge of the case, over its frame, so it's the first thing you see. Rare parts get a gold badge.

rounds.question: What should fill the dark strips beside the logo in the title glass?
rounds.found: Your painted logo is the old 4x4 shape and the radio's glass is now the wider 5x5 shape, so there's a strip each side. Five ways to deal with it, none of them stretch the painting. Pictures on a computer, a phone and the Retroid's screen; play opens the title with that option.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: your painted glass at its true shape, with a dark strip down each side of the wider 5x5 glass.

options.title: Blank keys
options.note: The painting's own blank corner keys carry on out to the frame on both sides, lined up with each row, so the grid just looks wider. Nothing is stretched; the logo stays exactly as painted.

options.title: Soft edges
options.note: The strips stay, but they glow faintly and the painting's edges melt into them, so there's no hard black bar. The smallest change.

options.title: Thicker frame
options.note: The radio's own wood from just outside the glass is copied inside at its true size, so the opening fits the picture: the frame looks a little heavier.

options.title: Band scales
options.note: A lit tuning scale fills each strip, like the station markings on an old radio: kilocycles down the left, megacycles down the right.

options.title: Zoom to fill
options.note: The picture is enlarged to fill the glass. No strips, but the tops of LEXI and the bottom of AL get cut. Shown so you can see why I'd avoid it.

rounds.question: Which take on the dot glass letters do you like best?
rounds.found: Six takes on the look the game has now, each with one idea, plus today's look for comparison. Every video is the same ten seconds: RAT is traced and becomes a word, it is sent and reaches the tower, new keys fall in, four letters are picked and taken back. The play links open the game with RAT traced in that look. All of them draw as fast as today's look or a little faster (measured at 640x480 on a slowed-down processor). Ideas can be combined: say which ones you want together. Chris picked deep glass with the clear path arrows and the lift-off together; that is now the game's look.

options.title: Dot glass (now)
options.note: The game as it is today, for comparison: flat dark keys, the line through the letters, the light wipe over a real word, letters breaking into dots when sent, keys scrambling as they land.

options.title: Deep glass
options.note: Richer glass. Every key sits in a recessed well (dark under its top lip, the lower lip catching the light), each letter throws a soft glow on the dots round it, and the pane gets a faint curved reflection, darker corners and a glint that slides across now and then. Plays exactly the same.

options.title: Warm-up
options.note: Keys power on as they arrive. A falling key rides dark; when it seats, its whole letter strikes on with a short stutter (dark, a white flash, dim, then settling to amber) instead of the scramble of dots. The start of a night and every refill look like the set warming up.

options.title: Word lock
options.note: A stronger real-word moment. When the letters become a word every key of it flashes together, a ring of light opens out from each, the keys get a thick pale-gold frame and breathe as one, and the rest of the glass dips so the word stands alone. Replaces the light wipe.

options.title: Clear path
options.note: The traced order without anything crossing a letter. Lit links run from the edge of one key to the edge of the next and end in an arrowhead, a bead runs along each link, and a lit stud marks the first key. Replaces the line through the middles and the ring.

options.title: Lift-off
options.note: A more satisfying send. The letters rise whole off the glass, bigger and brighter, while the fill drains away down the keys under them and an ember of each letter fades; then they come apart into dots from up there, with a few sparks, and stream to the tower. The send takes about a tenth of a second longer.

options.title: Side meter
options.note: Deeper, more orange amber, and the value moved out of the letter's dot field: a stack of four small lamp sockets in the right edge of each key, one lit per value step, so the letter stands alone and the value reads like a little level meter.

rounds.question: How should the title menu look under the radio?
rounds.found: Five ways, four of them with each option in its own container on dark floorboards (no bare black). Pictures for a computer and a phone; play links open the title with that look (left/right or up/down to choose, A to pick).

options.title: Bar and parchment (now)
options.note: What you didn't like, for comparison: the game's wood-and-brass bar across the bottom with one parchment holding the list.

options.title: Brass plates
options.note: Dark floorboards under the sideboard, each option on its own brass plate side by side. The chosen one is lit from behind with a red arrow; the other sits in shadow.

options.title: Station buttons
options.note: Each option is a big cream push button, like the preset keys on an old radio. The chosen one is pressed in and glows amber.

options.title: Dial windows
options.note: Each option is its own little lit display in a brass rim, lettered in the radio's dot-matrix lights. The chosen one burns bright; the other is dim.

options.title: Parchment tags
options.note: Each option is a parchment tag hanging from the radio's base on brass chains. The chosen one is lit and sways gently.

rounds.question: How should the Carrier Lamp's red key look?
rounds.found: Five ways to mark the red key (it doubles any word that uses it), all without the red outline. Each clip shows the key on its own, then picked into a word: every look keeps it red when picked. Play links open the game with the Carrier Lamp fitted.

options.title: Red letter
options.note: The key's letter is lit red instead of amber, with a soft red glow round it. Picked, it fills red.

options.title: Red backlight
options.note: The letter stays amber; the dots behind it glow a dim, breathing red, like a red bulb behind the panel.

options.title: Ember fill
options.note: A low red glow sits in the bottom of the key and gently rises and falls, like embers.

options.title: Pilot lamp
options.note: A small red pilot lamp in the key's corner, softly pulsing, and its value dots turn red. The quietest of the five.

options.title: Red scan
options.note: A red line keeps sweeping down the key, like a signal being picked up.

rounds.question: Which title screen should the game open on?
rounds.found: Six ways in. The bar is now away on the title screen and rises into place with a clunk when you start. Options 1-5 use a placeholder logo made from the game's own letters (the real one drops into the same spot later); 6 spells the title in the radio's keys. Watch the clips, or play each one: press A once to skip the entrance, again to start. You can mix pieces.

options.title: Tuning in
options.note: The room starts dark with static and the dial hunting. Scrambled letters flicker and lock into the logo left to right, it lands with a thump, then the six lamps come on one by one.

options.title: From the tower
options.note: Rings of red signal leave the tower's beacon and wash across the room. The logo forms out of wavy lines that settle into the letters, then it burns in.

options.title: Neon across the street
options.note: The logo is a neon sign on a dark board. The letters buzz on one at a time, stutter, and flood the room red; SIGNAL lights up in amber under it.

options.title: Fill the tube
options.note: The signal tube along the bar fills itself cell by cell. When it's full the room flashes and the logo drops in on a brass plate with a heavy clunk and a bounce.

options.title: Programme sheet
options.note: Parchment, like the old title box: a sheet slides up, the logo is stamped onto it, SIGNAL comes up in red ink and the two lines of how to play type out.

options.title: Radio close-up
options.note: Your sketch, with your painted glass. No bar, the radio big and centred (a clean 1.5x). Static in the glass, then each letter of your picture switches on in reading order with a stutter and a blip; once lit they breathe, and now and then one flickers out for a moment. The dial scrolls, the meter swings up, the lamps come on and a brass PRESS START plate appears.

rounds.question: How should a gold, one-time part look different from the regular parts, on its picker card and in its slot?
rounds.found: Chris wants more one-time gold parts, and the gold key's card and slot barely look different from the others now. Each option shows the picker (the Gold Key is the middle card) and the bar with the Gold Key fitted in the third slot. The cards' label also changes from RARE: ONCE ONLY to GOLD PART: ONE ONLY. All are drawn once and cached, except the glint, which only draws while it sweeps.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: A thin yellow line round the card and a soft glow; the slot looks like any other.

options.title: Gilded
options.note: The case frame, its name plate and the part's slot frame are recolored from brass to bright gold, pixel by pixel (the art's own shading kept), with a soft gold glow behind the slot.

options.title: Gilded + glint
options.note: Gilded, and every few seconds a band of light sweeps along the gold frame of the card and the slot. Watch the videos.

options.title: Jewel box
options.note: Gilded, with a crimson velvet lining inside the case and the slot, like a jewelry box. Reads as special even at a glance on the bar.

options.title: Gold seal
options.note: The case and slot stay brass, but a round gold medallion with an engraved star sits on their top-right corner: a stamp that says this one is different.

options.title: All in
options.note: Gilded + glint + the gold seal together.

rounds.question: Which music should play under the game while you spell (the main play screen)?
rounds.found: Chris wants chill 1930s-40s jazz, low and smooth, like a band playing in the next room. All four are made by the game itself as it runs (synthesized, no recordings, so the game stays small and the music never repeats exactly), heard through a wall: the highs rolled off and a little room echo, with the room's rain under it, turned down to about a third of its old level (Chris found it too loud over the music; the game's rain gets the same cut when the music goes in). Each clip is 75 seconds. They're turned up here so you can hear them; in the game they'd sit low under the rain. Pick one (or mix: say what you like from each) and I'll tune it in a second round. Decided 2026-11-14: none of them. Chris keeps the game's own music, since its tones match the game's sounds; the rain was turned down instead.

options.title: Piano trio, late ballad
options.note: Piano, brushes and an upright bass at 70 BPM, a slow minor tune with the piano taking the melody now and then.

options.title: Small band with a muted horn
options.note: A gentle swing at 96 BPM: walking bass, brushes and ride, piano chords, and a cup-muted trumpet playing short phrases every few bars.

options.title: Old 78 record through the wall
options.note: 84 BPM (your tempo): the band with a clarinet, as an old record would sound from the next room: narrow, warm, crackling, the pitch wavering slightly.

options.title: Vibraphone after hours
options.note: Very slow (62 BPM) and dreamy: a vibraphone with its tremolo over soft bass, the lightest brushes, a few piano chords.

rounds.question: How should each night start, so it's clear how much signal you need?
rounds.found: Chris: not enough clarity on how many points each night needs; a night intro you press past. Options 1-4 hold until you press A (or tap); the bar's top plate keeps showing what's left once you're playing. Every option shows the same facts: the night, the signal to beam, your words and retunes (parts that add to them are counted in), and the average a word needs. Shown on night 3 with a Spare Battery fitted. 'Play in game' opens that night with the card up.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: The brass plaque drops in at the top, holds about three seconds and lifts away by itself; any press sends it off sooner.

options.title: Big brass plaque
options.note: A large brass plaque over the dimmed room: NIGHT 3, the signal to beam in big red stamped figures, the words and retunes you have, and about how much each word needs to average. It waits for A.

options.title: Night ledger
options.note: A parchment card like the log: the night's terms on ruled lines (signal to beam, words, retunes, about a word), with what your parts add noted on their line. It waits for A.

options.title: On the radio's glass
options.note: The letters go dark and the glass itself lights up with the goal in the dial's dot lettering, the big number in the middle; the room stays lit. It waits for A.

options.title: Full-screen title card
options.note: The whole screen goes dark like an old film's title card: NIGHT THREE, a red beacon dot, the target big in cream, then you have 7 words and 1 retune, about 19 a word. It waits for A.

rounds.question: How should the bar and the run score stand out from the room, without making the room darker?
rounds.found: Chris: make our interface stand out over the background a bit more without darkening it or breaking anything. Each option is cheap (a few fills a frame, or one grayed copy of the room made once). 'Close up' shows the run score and the bar's top edge; 'Play in game' opens a word in progress with that option.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: The bar and the run score sit straight on the room, lit like the room.

options.title: Cast shadow
options.note: A soft shadow falls on the room just above the bar and under the run score, as if they stand in front of the wall.

options.title: Rim of lamplight
options.note: A warm line of light along the bar's top edge and the run score's top, as if the lamp catches their brass.

options.title: Dark keyline
options.note: A thin dark line round the run score and along the top of the bar, separating them from the room like a printed outline.

options.title: Room less colorful
options.note: The room (wallpaper, radio, sideboard, window) a little grayer at the same brightness, so the warm brass and parchment read stronger. Made once, costs nothing per frame.

options.title: Shadow and rim
options.note: Options 1 and 2 together.

rounds.question: How should the game warn you that you're on your last word and still short?
rounds.found: Every option starts the same way: once the turn before it is over, the dial flashes LAST WORD in (three quick blinks, then it holds, then blinks out), and while you play it scrolls LAST WORD * NEED 113. That's the new dial rule for everything important: it flashes in, centered; extras scroll. Each video starts with two words left, drops to the last word, then a word is traced.

options.title: Red tube
options.note: The empty part of the signal tube glows red and pulses, and the last battery lamp blinks red.

options.title: Fading signal
options.note: Static creeps over the glass, a torn line flicks across it now and then, and a key drops out for a moment: the radio is losing the station.

options.title: Heartbeat
options.note: The edges of the screen pulse dark red in a double beat, with a low thump you can hear (the video has no sound).

options.title: Red tube, light static
options.note: Option 1's red tube with a lighter version of option 2's static on the glass.

rounds.question: Fading signal, with more glitching on the letters: right amount?
rounds.found: Now in the game (build 203). A few keys at a time glitch for a few frames: a key drops out, a key tears with bright and dark lines, or a key splits red and blue. Keys in the word you're tracing (and the key under the cursor) never glitch, so it stays playable.

options.title: More glitching
options.note: The dial's LAST WORD flash here uses look 1 of the dial topic.

rounds.question: What should happen when the last lamp goes out and the night is lost?
rounds.found: Each takes about six seconds and any press skips it. The videos run on into the game over screen (the sheet, option 1 of the next topic). Sounds: pops, a falling whine, hiss, thuds.

options.title: Power down
options.note: The glass keys die one by one with little pops, the dial garbles into static and goes flat, the tube drains, then the room goes dark except the tower's red light blinking outside.

options.title: Signal lost
options.note: The dial flashes SIGNAL LOST, the tower's red light stutters and goes out, static floods the screen, then the picture squeezes to a bright line and a dot like an old set switching off.

options.title: Letters fall
options.note: The dial goes to a red flat line and every key drops out of the glass, one column at a time with a thud, then the room dims.

rounds.question: Power down into the sign-off log, over the dark room: right?
rounds.found: Now in the game (build 203). After the power-down the room stays nearly black with the tower's red light blinking, the dial stays dead, and the sign-off log prints up over it.

rounds.question: Which game over screen, and which title (GAME OVER, OFF THE AIR, SIGN-OFF or DEAD AIR)?
rounds.found: All three show the run score (with NEW HIGH SCORE when it is one), nights cleared, words sent, best word, longest word and everything that was on your radio, then NEW RUN and MAIN MENU (left / right and A, or tap). The buttons wake once the numbers are in, so you can't press through by accident. Any title can go on any layout.

options.title: Game over sheet
options.note: A parchment sheet like the night report, titled GAME OVER: the run score lit big, how the night ended, the run's numbers and every key and part you had (with x2, x3 for copies and LV2 and up for keys).

options.title: Off the air plaque
options.note: A brass plaque over the dark radio, titled OFF THE AIR, the run score stamped big.

options.title: Sign-off log
options.note: A printed station log feeds up out of the bar like a receipt, titled SIGN-OFF, ending with THANKS FOR LISTENING.

rounds.question: How should the dial grab your eye for important warnings and news?
rounds.found: Only important messages get this (LAST WORD, OVERDRIVE, and later ones like it); everyday ones (word scores, TOO SHORT) just flash in. Each video: LAST WORD (a warning, red), then OVERDRIVE (good news, amber).

options.title: Lit flash
options.note: The whole dial flashes lit (red for warnings, amber for good news) with dark letters, three times, then holds.

options.title: Glow
options.note: A big glow pulses around the dial and onto the radio while the message shows.

options.title: Scan line
options.note: A bright scan line sweeps across and writes the message in, then it holds.

options.title: Rim light
options.note: The dial's rim lights up and pulses, and the radio gives a small jolt.

options.title: Lit flash and glow
options.note: Options 1 and 2 together.

rounds.question: How should the radio switch on at the start of a run?
rounds.found: A new run now starts with the radio off: the glass dark, no lamps, the dial dead, under the NIGHT 1 plaque. Once you press A the radio powers on and the letters fall in (the falling sound you like stays). Only on night 1; later nights keep their letters. In each video the plaque shows, A is pressed, then the power-up.

options.title: Warm-up
options.note: A click and a rising hum; the glass warms from the middle like a valve heating, the battery lamps light one by one with rising notes, the dial says ON THE AIR, then the letters fall in column by column.

options.title: Tune in
options.note: A click, then static fills the glass while the dial scrolls up the stations (88.1 FM ... 97.6 FM); it locks with a chord, ON THE AIR, all the lamps light at once and the letters rain in.

options.title: Lamp cascade
options.note: The battery lamps light left to right with rising notes, the glass glows up from below, then the letters fall in one key at a time, from the top left to the bottom right.

topics.title: Value dots that tell the truth

rounds.question: How should a key show what your parts add to its letter?
rounds.found: Each key's amber dots show what its letter is worth. These add what your parts give it: the Vowel Antenna (+1 a copy on vowels) and the Treble Slider (+5 a copy on letters worth 3+). The pictures have two Vowel Antennas and a Treble Slider fitted, so vowels show two extra dots. They're drawn as a few plain squares, so they cost nothing to run.

options.title: White dots, square on top
options.note: Each Vowel Antenna adds a white dot above a vowel's value dots; the Treble Slider puts a bigger cream square at the top of that column on letters worth 3+.

options.title: Teal dots, square in the corner
options.note: The same extra dots in teal, and the Treble Slider's square in the key's top left corner.

options.title: Corner marks
options.note: Everything parts add sits in the key's top left corner: a small dot per Vowel Antenna, then the Treble Slider's bigger square.

rounds.question: How should the lamp at the end of the tube show that your word will clear the night (or overdrive)?
rounds.found: Each video: a 2-letter start, then a word that clears the night lights the lamp; the word is let go, then the same word on a night where it would overdrive (red). Every new look also pings when the lamp lights.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: The small lamp at the end of the tube lights warm when your word will clear the night, red for overdrive.

options.title: Bigger and brighter
options.note: A bigger lamp with a much stronger glow that spills over the end of the bar, and a soft ping when it lights.

options.title: Spark and flare
options.note: When it lights, sparks fly and a white flash bursts from the lamp, then a light streak runs across it like a lens flare.

options.title: The tube answers
options.note: The bigger lamp, and a band of light runs along the tube into it, over and over, while your word will clear.

options.title: Lit tag
options.note: The lamp as it is now, plus a small lit tag above it that says CLEAR, or OVERDRIVE in red.

rounds.question: How should the ice and the blue key show what your word will do to them, and how should they break?
rounds.found: New rule, in the game now: use a frozen key without the blue key and all the ice breaks, and the blue key breaks too. It comes back on another plain key (never the red, gold or green key, never in the word you just sent) and starts over at x2 with no ice. At blue key level 4 the blue key holds its place and half the ice stays. Each video: a word over the ice without the blue key (danger), let go, a word through the blue key (reward), that word sent (the ice pays), some ice built back, then a word over the ice without the blue key sent (it all breaks and the blue key moves). The Overlap still shows danger (left) and reward (right) with a red key on the ice, the green middle key frozen, a gold key next door and corner marks: all of those are drawn on top and stay readable.

options.title: Hairline cracks
options.note: Danger: thin white cracks creep in from the edges of every frozen key and the blue key, and they tremble (the blue key most); its x chip is struck out. Reward: the same cracks fill with light and glints twinkle. Break: gray shards drop, the blue key bursts and a comet of light carries it to its new key.

options.title: Fault lines
options.note: Danger: jagged cracks run from each frozen key across to the blue key, flickering, so you see it all hangs together. Reward: the lines turn into light with beads running into the blue key. Cash-in: the beads rush in before the burst. Break: a crack races across the glass to where the blue key reforms.

options.title: Pressure
options.note: The loudest. Danger: heavy cracks, a hard shake, flakes dropping off, the keys darken and the chip blinks the x2 you'd fall back to. Reward: the ice fills up with light, the chip swells and lights up. Break: a white flash and chunky shards; the blue key's shards fly over and fit back together. In the game now.

options.title: Lights
options.note: The calm one. Danger: the ice and the blue key go dark and dull with gray cracks, like the light is dying. Reward: they blaze and a sheen runs over each key. Break: the ice crumbles down as dust; the blue key's light goes out and stutters on at its new key.

rounds.question: Fault lines with sound, and a louder loss: does every case sound and look right?
rounds.found: This video has the game's real sound: tap Play with sound under it (videos start muted). In order: a word through the blue key with no ice (a small two-note chime, x2); two misses (a cold tink as a key freezes at the end of each turn); a word through the blue key with ice (the ice bursts with a glassy shatter and a run of rising notes, one more note for each frozen key); then a word on the ice without the blue key (the crack, a sad falling two-note drop, the glass flinches red, the multiplier you had falls off in a red struck-out plate, and the key reforms with a soft chime). Once all eight keys are frozen, each miss gives a higher tink as the frost deepens.

options.title: Fault lines, all cases, with sound

rounds.question: How should the frozen keys and the blue key look at rest, when your word isn't touching them?
rounds.found: The rules are unchanged; this is only the resting look. Each video has the game's sound (tap Play with sound): the board at rest with three frozen keys, a word that misses the blue key (one more key freezes at the end of the turn), then everything the blue key can reach frozen and the frost deepened three times (x13), then a trace over the ice without the blue key and letting go, to show the hand-over to the fault-line cracks and back. In every look the blue key's glow grows with what it holds, new ice grows in from the key's edges, ice about to shatter keeps its look until it goes, and a picked key shows its normal lit look. Nothing is drawn in a key's top left corner (the corner marks), frost on a key that is also the red, gold or green key is halved, and the red key, the gold key, the green ring and both chips are drawn on top: see each Overlap still (green middle key frozen, red and gold keys beside the ice, corner marks). Frame time at 640x480 with all eight frozen: every look within about half a millisecond of option 0.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: Frozen keys: blue letters and one small frost sprig in the top left corner (it sits under a corner mark when there is one). The blue key: a blue tint, two sprigs, its glow and the x chip.

options.title: Frosted panes
options.note: Each frozen key sits under a pale pane of frosted glass with a couple of glints; every few seconds a soft sheen crosses the ice from left to right. The blue key gets a deeper blue pane that brightens as it holds more. Deepened frost: a white frosted edge and specks on every pane.

options.title: Rime
options.note: White frost sprigs grow out of the corners and a fringe creeps along the edges. It is thicker on every frozen key the more the blue key holds (a few keys: light; all eight: heavy; deepened: heaviest, with glints twinkling). The blue key carries a small snow crystal in its bottom left corner that grows with it.

options.title: Frost veins
options.note: A thin frost vein joins every frozen key to the blue key, and now and then a bead of light drifts along it into the blue key, so you can see the ice is the blue key's. Frozen keys get a light blue film. When you trace over the ice, the fault-line cracks run along the same veins; through the blue key, they light up. Deepened frost: the veins turn white and thicker and the beads come more often. This is the one in the game for now.

options.title: Ice blocks
options.note: Frozen keys become beveled blocks of ice, lit from the top left. The blue key gets a small level meter on its right edge: one segment for each key it can freeze, filling from the bottom; deepened frost turns the segments white one by one.

options.title: Cold light
options.note: No frost drawn at all: the frozen keys' own dot fields glow cold blue, the blue key brightest, breathing slowly outward from the blue key. Deepened frost: the fields turn paler and brighter.

topics.title: A word that's good to send

rounds.question: With a lot going on, how should the game make it obvious a word is good to send?
rounds.found: Everything that already shows a good word stays; each option adds one thing. Every video is the same busy glass (the blue key with ice, the green key, the red and gold keys): it traces a few letters, makes a word and holds it, adds a letter that breaks it, takes it back, then sends. The videos have the game's sound: tap Play with sound. Options can be combined: say which in a note.

options.title: As now (nothing added)
options.note: For comparison: what already shows a good word. The keys light and a light sweeps across them, the dial lights warm with a + on the number, the tube blinks the cells it would fill, and a short two-note lock sound.

options.title: Dial lock-on
options.note: The moment the letters make a word, the dial flashes lit twice, then a warm glow pulses round it (and spills onto the top of the glass) for as long as the word holds. Uses the same glow you picked for important dial messages.

options.title: Tuning eye
options.note: A round green tuning tube set into the cabinet above the right grille, like the tuning eye on an old set. Dim and open while you trace; when the letters make a word its dark wedge snaps shut and it glows bright green. Opens again the moment the word breaks.

options.title: Send lamp
options.note: A small SEND lamp sign above the left grille. Dark while you trace; when the letters make a word it strikes on like a neon sign (a couple of flickers, then steady red-orange glow). Goes dark the moment the word breaks.

options.title: Focus lock
options.note: Four bright corner brackets fly in and lock onto the corners of the glass when the letters make a word, with a quick flash round the rim. They stay, softly pulsing, while the word holds, and slide away when it breaks.

options.title: Hot path
options.note: The trace itself goes white-hot and thicker when it's a word, and the word's keys beat together with a bright rim, like a heartbeat. Everything happens on the word, so your eye doesn't leave the glass.

options.title: Send tag
options.note: A lit SEND tag appears on the last letter (where pressing A again sends), bobbing gently; on a touch screen it says TAP. It hangs below the key (above it on the bottom row), so it can sit over part of the key below.

rounds.question: Your idea: the dial blinks between reverse print and normal while the word holds. Does it read?
rounds.found: Option 1's warm glow stays round the dial, and the dial itself swaps between reverse print (lit field, dark letters) and normal every half second, like a blinking cursor, for as long as the letters make a word. It stops the moment the word breaks. Same busy glass and the same moves as round 1, with a longer hold on the word so you see several blinks. Tap Play with sound.

rounds.question: Round 2's reverse blink was a bit much: which calmer take reads clearly without shouting?
rounds.found: Same busy glass and moves as before, with a long hold on the word. Every option keeps what the game already shows for a good word (lit keys, the light sweep, the + on the number, the tube cells, the lock sound). Tap Play with sound.

options.title: Reverse blink (as in the game now, fixed)
options.note: What's in the game now: the warm glow round the dial, and the dial blinking between reverse print and normal every half second. Fixed: the reverse print now stays inside the dial's window, so it no longer lights over the bezel.

options.title: Soft wash blink
options.note: No big glow. The dial window takes a soft warm wash every half second (about a third as bright as full reverse); the letters stay bright amber the whole time.

options.title: Slow breathe
options.note: No glow. The dial fades smoothly into reverse print and back out again over about a second and a half, instead of a hard blink.

options.title: Just the word, reversed
options.note: No glow. Only the word gets a lit box behind it (dark letters on amber) that blinks on and off every half second, like selected text. The number stays as it is.

options.title: Two blinks, then steady
options.note: Two quick reverse blinks the moment the letters make a word, then the dial stays normal with a soft steady glow for as long as the word holds. No continuous blinking.

options.title: Blinking cursor
options.note: No glow. A solid block cursor blinks right after the word on the dial, every half second, the way a text cursor does when it's waiting for you.

topics.title: The gold key, easy to spot

rounds.question: How should the gold key stay obviously gold, even once its letter locks into a word?
rounds.found: Each video: the glass at rest, then a word traced through the gold key (its letter locks in), held, and sent. The stills show it at rest, traced, and where it overlaps: one gold key sitting on the green key and one that's also the red key.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison. At rest the gold key spins its letter reel in a gold frame with two little arrows; once a word goes through it the letter locks in and it looks almost like any other traced key.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Gold letter
options.note: The gold key's letters are always gold (the spinning reel and the letter it locks to), a richer gold while traced, so it never turns into a plain key.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Gold shimmer
options.note: A gold sheen sweeps across the key every second and a half, at rest and while traced (brighter while traced).

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Shake
options.note: The key jitters like a coin on a table: a short shake every few seconds at rest, and a steady small shake while it's in your word.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Gold setting
options.note: A thick polished gold frame with four studs at the corners, like a set jewel, always on; it glows while traced.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Gold letter + glow
options.note: Option 1's gold letters, plus a soft gold glow behind the key that grows while it's traced.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

options.title: Gold plate
options.note: The whole key face is solid gold with a dark letter (a red letter when it's also the red key), at rest and traced. The boldest.

images.label: Overlaps: on the green key, and also the red key

rounds.question: Which look for the green key reads best, without getting in the way of the other keys?
rounds.found: Each video: the glass at rest, then a word traced through the green key, held, and sent (the charge goes up). The stills show it at rest, traced, and with things overlapping it: the green key is also the red key, the gold key sits next to it, and there's ice around.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: the green ring round the middle key and its charge number on a tag.

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

options.title: Green letter
options.note: The ring and tag stay; the green key's letter also glows green (a red or gold letter wins if the key is also red or gold).

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

options.title: Charge bar
options.note: The ring and tag stay; a thin green bar inside the key's left edge fills up as the charge grows.

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

options.title: Battery tag
options.note: The ring stays; the charge tag becomes a little battery (with a terminal nub) that fills with green as the charge grows.

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

options.title: Breathing ring
options.note: The ring breathes in and out, slowly at first and faster and brighter as the charge grows.

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

options.title: Corner lamp
options.note: The ring and tag stay; a small round green lamp in the key's bottom-left corner glows brighter as the charge grows.

images.label: Overlaps: also the red key, next to gold and ice

rounds.question: When you send a word, where should the count-up play out?
rounds.found: Every option counts the same way, in order: the 2 every word carries; each letter's value (with any part's bonus on that letter); the length, and parts that make it longer; each multiplier, one at a time with a stamp; flat adds (green key, a request); then the total, and only then do the letters fly to the tower. It speeds up as it goes, and A, X or a tap skips to the total. The video's word is JOKER through the red key, with the Treble Slider (J and K), a Tube Amp, the Long Wave Coil (5 letters) and the green key's charge. Tap Play with sound.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: the score is added up instantly and the letters fly straight to the tower with the total.

options.title: On the dial
options.note: The count-up plays on the dial as a running sum: the signal climbs letter by letter (each letter flares on the glass as it's counted), then x the length, then each multiplier, then the flat adds, with the running total on the right. Each part's slot flashes with its tag the moment it adds in.

options.title: On the keys
options.note: The count-up plays on the glass: each letter pops its value on a little chip as it's counted, part bonuses pop on their letter, the length and multipliers stamp over the word in big chips (red for multipliers, green for the green key's charge), and the total pops at the end. Slots flash as their part adds in.

options.title: Both
options.note: The chips on the keys and the running sum on the dial together.

rounds.question: Building on Both: what makes it easiest to follow, parts and all?
rounds.found: Every video is the whole screen now, bar included, so you can watch the parts' slots flash (with their tags rising) while it counts. The word is JOKER through the red key with the Treble Slider, a Tube Amp, the Long Wave Coil and the green key's charge. Tap Play with sound.

options.title: Both, as in round 1
options.note: For comparison: chips on the keys and the running sum on the dial, now seen with the whole screen, bar and all.

options.title: Sparks from the parts
options.note: When a part adds in, its slot in the bar flares and a spark flies from it to where it lands: to the letter for a letter bonus (the Treble Slider's +5 on the J), to the dial for length, multipliers and the green key's charge. You can follow each part's effect from its slot.

options.title: Tidy chips
options.note: Less on the glass at once: each letter's chip fades quickly, and only the latest length or multiplier chip stays over the word, so a busy word doesn't pile up.

options.title: The tube fills live
options.note: The signal tube along the bar fills with the running total as it counts up, so you see the night's progress grow with every step.

options.title: All three
options.note: Sparks, tidy chips and the live tube together.

rounds.question: Slow with sparks leading: score the parts as they come, or the plain word first?
rounds.found: Slow, and each part's spark leads its step, in the order the score is worked out. The length is one chip, "5 LETTERS X3", and the Tube Amp's spark turns it into X4. The dial shows the plain math in step (no sparks go there), and when the signal reaches the tower nothing flashes again. A, X or a tap skips to the total. Tap Play with sound.

options.title: Parts as they come
options.note: Each letter, then any part bonus on that letter, then the length and the parts that make it longer, then the multipliers and the green key.

options.title: Plain word first
options.note: The word scores on its own first: the 2, every letter, "5 LETTERS X3" (JOKER alone: 15 x 3 = 45). Then the parts add on, each with its spark: Treble Slider +5 to the J and the K, the Tube Amp turns X3 into X4, the Coil x2, the red key x3, the green key +19. Same total; you see what your word was worth and what your radio added.

rounds.question: How should the count-up be split up and sound, without getting longer?
rounds.found: All on top of the count-up you picked (the plain word first, then each part with its spark). Same word: JOKER through the red key with the Treble Slider, a Tube Amp, the Coil and the green key's charge. Turn the sound up: tap Play with sound.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: the count-up in the game now, at one even pace with the old sounds.

options.title: Phases
options.note: The count splits into its parts: the word, the letter bonuses, the length, the multipliers, the adds. Each part goes a little quicker, with a short beat between parts. Soft simple sounds: a light tick per letter, a whoosh as a spark leaves its slot, a small bell when it lands, a low thump for each multiplier, a warm chord at the end. About the same length overall.

options.title: Phases + roll-up
options.note: Like 1, and when the plain word is done its chips gather into one tag over the word ("JOKER 45") with a two-note chime, so you see what the word alone was worth before the parts start.

options.title: Phases, one tune
options.note: Like 1, but every sound is a note in one scale that climbs through the whole count: the letters walk up, the parts keep climbing, multipliers ring lower and fuller, and the final chord resolves it.

options.title: Roll-up + tune
options.note: 2 and 3 together.
